title: Winning Time: Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces and the New Dimension of War
gist: Former Ukrainian PM Oleksiy Honcharuk argues adaptation speed has become the decisive contest in the Russo-Ukrainian war, which he names the 'Time Domain', and that Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces (about 2.5% of personnel, roughly a third of Russian losses) and 'Combat Hub' units are the force structure built to win it. He urges NATO and the US to buy adaptation cycles rather than platforms and to treat visible adaptation capacity as a new form of deterrence.

insights.claim: Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, created in late 2023 as the world's first dedicated military branch for unmanned systems, make up about 2.5% of Ukraine's military personnel but accounted for roughly a third of Russian losses in the past year.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: Extreme cost-effectiveness of drone formations supports sustained demand for drone makers and a structural reallocation of defense budgets toward unmanned systems.
insights.quote: A force with about 2.5 percent of Ukraine’s military personnel has accounted for roughly a third of Russian losses this past year.
insights.locator: In late 2023, Ukraine’s military leadership

insights.claim: Most of Ukraine's career generals opposed creating a separate unmanned systems branch on the doctrinal grounds that every branch needs its own physical domain, while the advocates were mostly newcomers from civilian life with a culture of continuous experimentation and tolerance of failure.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: Institutional resistance from legacy military culture is a key friction slowing Western adoption of unmanned forces; watch where civilian-tech talent gains influence in procurement.
insights.quote: No domain, no branch of service.

insights.claim: In its first seven months, the strike-copter project that became Ukraine's 412th Brigade 'Nemesis' flew over 950 sorties with 47 crews, destroying more than 520 targets including over 360 pieces of equipment valued at $308 million, while losing 107 airframes worth about $3.2 million, roughly a 100:1 exchange ratio in dollar terms.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: A ~100:1 cost-exchange ratio for heavy strike drones versus armored equipment undermines the investment case for expensive legacy platforms; figures are from the unit's own flight records, not public data.
insights.quote: roughly a hundred dollars of destroyed Russian equipment for every dollar of airframe lost
insights.locator: The Combat Hub: Ukraine’s New Type

insights.claim: The heavy strike copter at the core of the 412th Brigade 'Nemesis' evolved from first models carrying about six kilograms over 10 kilometers to latest versions reaching nearly 100 kilometers.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: Rapid range growth of cheap strike drones extends the threat envelope deep behind front lines, raising demand for counter-drone and air-defense systems.
insights.locator: The Combat Hub: Ukraine’s New Type

insights.claim: Lasar's Group, a Ukrainian National Guard unit that started in 2022 as a self-funded volunteer drone team, is credited with destroying $12 billion worth of Russian equipment.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: Bottom-up volunteer units can generate outsized combat effect, suggesting defense value increasingly accrues to small agile producers rather than primes.
insights.quote: credited with destroying $12 billion worth of Russian equipment
insights.locator: The pattern extends beyond one brigade

themes.theme: Time Domain: adaptation speed as the decisive contest

insights.claim: The decisive dimension of the war in Ukraine is not where forces fight but how fast each side adapts: mass decides how long a side can keep paying, while speed determines how much each payment buys.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: Investors should value defense suppliers by iteration speed and update cadence, not just volume of hardware delivered.
insights.quote: Mass decides how long a side can continue to pay, and speed determines how much each payment buys.
insights.locator: The decisive dimension of the war

insights.claim: The author proposes the 'Time Domain' as a sixth operational domain: a competition for the interval between a new capability reaching the front and the enemy's working counter, which is measurable, spendable and compounding, and therefore needs an owner with its own doctrine, command and budget.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: If NATO adopts this framing, budget lines and capability targets would shift toward rapid-iteration programs and software-defined attritable systems.
insights.quote: Treat the contest for time as an attribute of the others, and it becomes everyone’s concern and no one’s mission.

insights.claim: The window between a new system appearing at the front and an effective enemy counter now sometimes lasts only weeks, and that compression of the cycle from years to weeks is what makes the interval itself the contest.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: Weapon systems face rapid obsolescence; favor suppliers with modular, updatable architectures over monolithic platforms.
insights.quote: The window between a new system appearing at the front and an effective enemy counter sometimes lasts only weeks.

insights.claim: The author extends John Boyd's OODA-loop insight from individual engagements to the entire military organism, spanning observation, engineering, production and back into combat.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: Defense-tech firms that integrate battlefield data loops with production are positioned for the next procurement paradigm.
insights.locator: Tempo and operational speed describe

insights.claim: Ukrainian combat drone units run a 'Combat Hub' model fusing combat operations, analytics, R&D and production under one command, iterating on three horizons: daily fixes, six-week iterations and six-month generational changes.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: The six-week iteration cadence is a benchmark for evaluating defense-tech vendors and military innovation units.
insights.quote: daily fixes, so the unit is sharper the next night; iterations every six weeks, so the next batch is better; and bigger changes every six months
insights.locator: I call this architecture the Combat Hub

insights.claim: RAND and Modern War Institute research found Ukraine's adaptation runs largely on fragile informal networks; the Combat Hub institutionalizes the cycle so it survives the loss of individuals and can be reproduced.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: Institutionalization determines whether battlefield innovation persists; watch for formal adoption of hub-like structures in allied militaries.
insights.locator: The Combat Hub matters beyond Ukraine

themes.theme: Russia and the US copying the model

insights.claim: Russia was first to field jam-proof fiber-optic drones at scale, around Kursk, via its Rubicon defense-ministry center, but its lead lasted only months: by April 2025 Ukraine had more than 20 certified fiber-optic drone models from 11 producers.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: Any single drone innovation's advantage is measured in months, favoring a broad, competitive producer base over single-vendor bets.
insights.quote: By April 2025, Ukraine had more than 20 certified fiber-optic models from 11 producers
insights.locator: Russia plays this game, too

insights.claim: Putin ordered Russia to create its own unmanned systems branch in December 2024, and by late 2025 Russia's Unmanned Systems Forces were operational, copying even Ukraine's name.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: Adversary emulation validates the organizational model, signaling a durable shift in force structure and drone procurement on both sides.
insights.locator: Russia plays this game, too

insights.claim: By the end of 2025, U.S. Central Command had fielded a one-way attack drone modeled on Iran's Shahed, after the U.S. Navy had to rewrite tactics as the Houthis escalated in the Red Sea from drones to anti-ship cruise and ballistic missiles.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: US adoption of cheap Shahed-style attack drones signals a budget market for low-cost attritable munitions in the US.
insights.quote: When the world’s most powerful military copies its adversary’s weapon to close an adaptation gap
insights.locator: Nor is the game confined

themes.theme: Prescriptions for NATO procurement and force structure

insights.claim: Western procurement should buy adaptation cycles rather than systems, favoring modular systems crews can update within a week over monolithic ones that take years to modify, and making direct operator-manufacturer feedback loops a contractual standard.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: Procurement reform along these lines would advantage software-defined, modular defense-tech firms over legacy primes with long upgrade cycles.
insights.quote: Procurement should buy adaptation cycles rather than systems.
insights.locator: Procurement should buy adaptation cycles

insights.claim: Unmanned systems should be organized as a dedicated branch rather than an innovation command across existing branches, because sea and air drones share procurement and adaptation cycles far more with each other than with crewed platforms; they cluster by adaptation cycle, not environment.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: Watch whether NATO members create standalone drone branches with their own budget lines, a direct demand signal for drone makers.
insights.quote: They cluster by adaptation cycle, not by environment
insights.locator: Why that player is a branch

insights.claim: Ukraine routes most drone money by effect: units earn points for Delta-verified strikes and spend them on drones, and brigades order directly from manufacturers through a marketplace built to carry 70 percent of drone procurement in 2026.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: A marketplace channeling 70% of drone procurement directly from producers rewards vendors on verified battlefield effect, a model allies may copy.
insights.quote: a marketplace built to carry 70 percent of drone procurement in 2026
insights.locator: What allies should look at

insights.claim: Large peacetime militaries should insulate a bounded enclave of about two percent of the force under different procurement and failure-tolerance rules, extending the U.S. Defense Innovation Unit approach from buying technology to fighting with it.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: Suggests a modest but protected budget slice for rapid-iteration units, a realistic entry point for defense startups in Western markets.
insights.quote: risking two percent to buy the other 98 percent the time in which to change
insights.locator: The fair objection is whether

insights.claim: Allied planning should add a temporal axis, tracking how long each friendly and enemy unit needs to go from identifying a new adversary tactic to fielding a countermeasure.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: Time-to-countermeasure could become a procurement metric that favors analytics and data-integration vendors.
insights.locator: Planning should acquire a temporal axis

insights.claim: The author sees a timely policy window because Europe is writing its next seven-year budget with defense as one of its largest new lines and NATO is rewriting its capability targets.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: EU multiannual budget and NATO capability-target decisions are the near-term catalysts for drone and autonomy procurement in Europe.
insights.quote: Europe is writing its next seven-year budget, with defense as one of its largest new lines
insights.locator: The moment has a calendar

themes.theme: Deterrence by adaptation and its risks

insights.claim: Visible adaptation capacity, such as hubs with their own engineers, drone marketplaces, public strike leaderboards and a legally established branch with a budget line, may deter like stockpiles once did by threatening an aggressor with obsolescence rather than punishment, though the author calls this an untested hypothesis.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: If adaptation capacity becomes a recognized deterrent, defense spending may tilt from inventory toward industrial and innovation capacity.
insights.quote: What it threatens is not punishment but obsolescence
insights.locator: There is a payoff beyond

insights.claim: The Strategic Defense Initiative is a precedent for deterrence by expected innovation: Soviet leaders reacted to what they believed America could build, not to any deployed system.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: Credible signaling of innovation capacity can move adversary behavior before fielding, so announced programs themselves have strategic and market impact.
insights.quote: What America had built did not deter Moscow — what it believed America could build did.
insights.locator: There is a precedent for deterrence

insights.claim: Drawing on prospect theory and Dale Copeland's reading of 1914, the author warns that a defender visibly gaining adaptation speed can provoke rather than deter, because an aggressor facing a closing window may strike early, so the capacity should be running before the aggressor looks.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: Rapid visible military modernization by Europe or Taiwan could raise near-term conflict risk; a geopolitical tail risk to price during build-up phases.
insights.quote: A window that has closed deters. A window that is closing invites.
insights.locator: Deterrence theory adds a warning here

insights.claim: Ukraine's adaptation speed rests on societal foundations, including decentralized command folding in businesses and volunteers, dispersed small producers that survive strikes, fast-scaling defense startups and an engaged population, which no ministry can build by decree.
insights.speaker: Oleksiy Honcharuk
insights.so_what: Ukraine's defense-startup ecosystem is a structural asset, but the model is hard to replicate in societies lacking similar self-organization.
insights.locator: A final lesson reaches beyond
